hints: Focus on the last two steps, because a white precipitate that disappears in excess NaOH is a very special clue.
Recall which metal hydroxide is amphoteric and dissolves in excess alkali to give a clear aluminate solution.
Work backwards to check that this metal also burns to a white oxide that dissolves in dilute HCl.
walkthrough:
**Follow the sequence from Y to the oxide**

Y burns in oxygen to give a white solid. For metals like Na, Mg and Al this is the metal oxide. Think of it as the starting test for the oxide behaviour.

Example: $$4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$

**Dissolve the oxide in acid**

The white solid dissolves in $\text{HCl(aq)}$ to give a solution. This tells us the oxide is basic or amphoteric, forming the metal chloride.

Example: $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Add NaOH to get the hydroxide precipitate**

Adding $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to that solution gives a white precipitate of the metal hydroxide.

Example: $$\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\text{NaCl}$$

**Use excess NaOH as the key test**

The white precipitate then dissolves in an excess of $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to give a clear solution. Only an amphoteric hydroxide does this, forming a soluble complex anion.

Example: $$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}$$
This amphoteric behaviour points straight to aluminium.

options.A: Sodium burns to a white solid $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ which dissolves in HCl to give $\text{NaCl}$ solution, but adding NaOH gives no precipitate because $\text{NaOH}$ is very soluble. The sequence fails at the white precipitate stage.
options.B: Magnesium fits the first part well: $\text{MgO}$ (white solid) to $\text{MgCl}_2$ (solution) to $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ (white precipitate). However $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is basic only, not amphoteric, so it does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This is the classic trap.
options.C: Aluminium fits every step perfectly. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is a white solid, dissolves in HCl to $\text{AlCl}_3$, gives white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ precipitate with NaOH, and this amphoteric hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH to give soluble $\text{[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}^-$.
options.D: Phosphorus burns to white $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ which dissolves in water or acid to give acidic phosphate solution. Adding NaOH would give soluble sodium phosphate, not a white precipitate. It fails the precipitate test.
